title: Imperialism and World Economy
author: Nikolai Bukharin
context: Written in 1915 during World War I with an introduction by V.I. Lenin and published in 1917, Imperialism and World Economy is Nikolai Bukharin's landmark Marxist study of global monopoly capitalism. Bukharin analyzes the dual dialectical process of the internationalization of economic life and the nationalization (statification) of capital into competing 'state-capitalist trusts', demonstrating why monopoly competition inevitably escalates from protective tariffs and capital export into militarism and world war.
relatesToToday: Bukharin's framework of 'state-capitalist trusts' and the fusion of monopoly finance capital with national state power explains modern geopolitical rivalry, trade wars, supply-chain blockades, sovereign wealth competition, and military-industrial conflicts over strategic raw materials and global sales markets.
keyTakeaways: The growth of the world division of labor internationalizes capital while simultaneously fusing national monopolies with state power into 'state-capitalist trusts'.
Free competition does not vanish under monopoly capitalism; it is displaced from the domestic market onto the world arena in far more destructive forms.
High protective tariffs evolve from defensive shields for infant industries into aggressive weapons enabling cartels to extract domestic superprofits and dump goods abroad.
Karl Kautsky's reformist theory of 'ultra-imperialism' (a peaceful world trust) is a utopian illusion contradicted by uneven capitalist development.
Imperialist war is the inevitable continuation of the economic struggle of state-capitalist trusts over sales markets, raw materials, and spheres of capital investment.
